title: What are the common sharding strategies — hash-based (consistent hashing on shard key — even distribution, hard range queries), range-based (date/ID ranges — easy range scans, risk of hot partitions), directory-based (lookup table maps key→shard — flexible, single point of lookup) — and how do you choose the shard key (high cardinality, even distribution, aligned with query patterns)?
shortTitle: Common sharding strategies and choosing a shard key

s1_definition.profdef: Sharding splits one logical dataset across many physical databases (shards) to scale beyond a single node. Hash-based sharding hashes the shard key for even distribution but makes range queries hard; range-based sharding assigns contiguous key ranges, making range scans easy but risking hot partitions; directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table mapping keys to shards for flexibility at the cost of a lookup dependency. A good shard key has high cardinality, distributes evenly, and matches the dominant query pattern.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has too many accounts for one database, so it spreads them across several. Hash-based is like assigning accounts to branches by a scrambling formula so every branch is equally full. Range-based is like branch A keeps accounts 1 to a million — easy to grab a range, but if all new accounts land in the last branch it gets overloaded. Directory-based is like a central register that says exactly which branch holds Rajesh's account — flexible but you always consult the register first.
s1_definition.oneliner: Hash spreads evenly but kills range scans; range enables scans but risks hotspots; directory is flexible but adds a lookup — pick the shard key by cardinality, evenness, and query pattern.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sharding splits one logical dataset across many physical databases (shards) to scale beyond a single node. Hash-based sharding hashes the shard key for even distribution but makes range queries hard; range-based sharding assigns contiguous key ranges, making range scans easy but risking hot partitions; directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table mapping keys to shards for flexibility at the cost of a lookup dependency. A good shard key has high cardinality, distributes evenly, and matches the dominant query pattern.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has too many accounts for one database, so it spreads them across several. Hash-based is like assigning accounts to branches by a scrambling formula so every branch is equally full. Range-based is like branch A keeps accounts 1 to a million — easy to grab a range, but if all new accounts land in the last branch it gets overloaded. Directory-based is like a central register that says exactly which branch holds Rajesh's account — flexible but you always consult the register first.

**One line to remember:** Hash spreads evenly but kills range scans; range enables scans but risks hotspots; directory is flexible but adds a lookup — pick the shard key by cardinality, evenness, and query pattern.

sections.s2_technical:
Hash-based: `shard = hash(key) % N`, or consistent hashing to limit movement when N changes. Distribution is even and single-key lookups are fast, but queries over a key range touch every shard (scatter-gather), and plain modulo reshuffles almost everything when N changes, which is why consistent hashing is preferred.

Range-based: assign contiguous ranges (account id blocks, date ranges). Range scans and time-window queries stay on few shards, and adding capacity is easy, but monotonically increasing keys create a hot shard where all new writes land, and skewed ranges unbalance load.

Directory-based: a lookup service maps each key to its shard, so you can place and relocate data freely and rebalance granularly; the cost is an extra lookup on every access and the directory becoming a critical, must-be-cached component.

Choosing the shard key: pick high cardinality so data spreads (account id, not branch city); pick even distribution to avoid hotspots; align with the dominant query so most queries hit a single shard — if lookups are by account, shard by account id; avoid keys that force cross-shard joins. Senior nuance: the shard key is very hard to change later, so model query patterns first; consider composite keys; and plan resharding (consistent hashing with virtual nodes) from day one.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's single accounts database is saturated. This is exactly sharding: distribute accounts across shards. We compare hash, range, and directory routing and show why hashing account id gives even spread for single-account lookups.

The demo has a `ShardRouter` with `hashRoute()`, `rangeRoute()`, and `directoryRoute()`, printing which shard Rajesh and Priya land on and illustrating the hot-partition risk of range routing.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
sharding-service/
├── pom.xml
└── src/main/java/com/bank/sharding/
    ├── ShardDemo.java
    ├── model/ShardKey.java
    └── service/ShardRouter.java
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__sharding_note.sql (each shard is a separate database with the SAME schema)
-- shard_0, shard_1, shard_2 each contain:
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,   -- shard key: high cardinality, even, queried by id
    holder  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
-- Routing happens in the application / proxy, not inside one DB.
-- Hash:      shard = hash(id) % 3
-- Range:     id 'SAV0000'..'SAV3333' → shard_0, etc.
-- Directory: SELECT shard FROM shard_map WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001';
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
sharding:
  strategy: hash           # hash | range | directory
  shards: [shard_0, shard_1, shard_2]
  shard-key: account_id
  virtual-nodes: 150       # for consistent hashing balance
```

```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests
# Run
java -cp target/sharding-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.sharding.ShardDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: two accounts, Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), routed by three strategies across three shards.

Step 1: hashRoute scrambles each account id and takes modulo three, scattering the two accounts evenly; a single-account lookup goes straight to one shard.

Step 2: rangeRoute maps by numeric id block, which keeps ranges together but warns that brand-new, ever-increasing ids all land on the last shard — the hot-partition risk.

Step 3: directoryRoute consults the explicit map after placing Rajesh on shard 2, showing flexible placement at the cost of a lookup.

```text
2026-10-25 18:40:00 [INFO] HASH SAV2001 -> shard_1
2026-10-25 18:40:00 [INFO] HASH CUR3001 -> shard_0
2026-10-25 18:40:00 [INFO] RANGE SAV2001 -> shard_0 (hot-shard risk on new ids)
2026-10-25 18:40:00 [INFO] DIRECTORY SAV2001 -> shard_2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  account id (shard key)
    │
    ├─ HASH: hash(id) % N        → even spread, single-key fast, range = scatter
    ├─ RANGE: id block → shard   → range scans easy, new ids → HOT shard
    └─ DIRECTORY: map[id]→shard  → flexible placement, +1 lookup
    ▼
  routed to shard_0 | shard_1 | shard_2
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sharding splits one logical dataset across many physical databases to scale past a single node, and the three common strategies trade off differently. Hash-based sharding hashes the shard key, usually with consistent hashing, giving even distribution and fast single-key lookups, but range queries must scatter-gather across every shard. Range-based sharding assigns contiguous key ranges so range and time-window scans stay on a few shards and capacity is easy to add, but monotonically increasing keys create a hot shard where all new writes pile up. Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table mapping each key to its shard, which allows flexible placement and granular rebalancing at the cost of an extra lookup on every access and a directory that must be highly available and cached.

Choosing the shard key is the most consequential decision because it is very hard to change later. I pick a key with high cardinality so data spreads out, that distributes evenly to avoid hotspots, and that aligns with the dominant query so most requests hit a single shard. In our National Bank of India accounts platform the overwhelming access pattern is lookup by account id, so I shard by account id using consistent hashing with virtual nodes, which spreads load evenly and keeps single-account reads on one shard; I avoid keys like branch city that would skew badly, and I plan resharding from day one. The line I remember is: hash spreads evenly but hurts range scans, range enables scans but risks hotspots, and directory is flexible but adds a lookup — so choose the shard key by cardinality, evenness, and query pattern.
